summary: Defines the Extensible Authentication Protocol for PPP, which lets PPP links use many authentication methods before network traffic is sent. It was replaced by RFC 3748.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a dial-up connection starts, you must prove who you are. This lets many different ways of proving it be used.

questions: how does eap work with ppp
what are the eap packet codes
subtitle: A PPP authentication method that lets the link pick the actual login scheme only after it is up.

tldr.problem: PPP normally negotiates one fixed authentication protocol while the link is being set up, which makes it hard to use new methods or to ask the user for more information first.
tldr.mechanism: EAP negotiates only that EAP will be used, then the authenticator sends Request packets and the peer answers with Responses of a chosen type (identity, MD5-challenge, one-time password, token card), ending with Success or Failure.
tldr.outcome: It was updated by RFC 2484 and replaced by RFC 3748.

today: RFC 2284 is obsolete. It was updated by RFC 2484 and replaced by RFC 3748.

sections.title: Authenticating a PPP Link
sections.content:
After PPP's Link Establishment phase, there is an optional Authentication phase before network traffic flows. Authentication is not mandatory by default. To require it, an implementation MUST specify the Authentication-Protocol Configuration Option during link establishment.

The protocols are mainly meant for hosts and routers that connect to a PPP network server by switched circuits or dial-up lines. The server may use the identity of the caller to choose options for network layer negotiation. This RFC defines the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) as one such protocol; the phases themselves come from RFC 1661.

Two terms matter: the authenticator is the end that requires the authentication, and the peer is the end being authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: When two computers connect over a phone line, one of them can insist that the other prove who it is first. The checker is the authenticator and the one being checked is the peer.

sections.title: How EAP Works
sections.content:
EAP does not choose a specific authentication mechanism during link setup. It postpones the choice to the Authentication phase, so the authenticator can ask for more information first. It also allows a "back-end" server to implement the mechanisms while the PPP authenticator just passes the exchange through.

  • The authenticator sends one or more Requests. Typically the first is an Identity Request, but it can be skipped where the identity is presumed, such as leased lines.
  • The peer answers each Request with a Response of a matching type.
  • The authenticator ends the phase with a Success or Failure packet.

The advantage is that many mechanisms work without being negotiated in advance, and a device such as a NAS only needs to look for the success or failure code. The disadvantage is that PPP implementations must be modified to add a new authentication type to LCP, and EAP departs from the older model of negotiating one mechanism up front.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of agreeing on the secret handshake before meeting, EAP lets the doorman ask for one at the door. The doorman may even call a boss in the back room who does the real checking.

sections.title: EAP Packets
sections.content:
The Authentication-Protocol option for EAP has Type 3, Length 4 and the protocol value C227 in hex. Exactly one EAP packet is carried in the Information field of a PPP frame whose protocol field is hex C227.

An EAP packet has a one-octet Code (1 Request, 2 Response, 3 Success, 4 Failure), a one-octet Identifier that matches responses to requests, a two-octet Length that covers the whole packet, and a Data field. Request and Response packets add a one-octet Type and Type-Data after the Length. Success and Failure packets have a Length of 4 and no more fields.
sections.plainLanguage: Every EAP message starts with a small label: what kind of message it is, a number to match answers with questions, and how long it is.

sections.title: Requests, Responses and Retries
sections.content:
The authenticator MUST send Requests until it gets a valid Response or an optional retry counter expires. A retransmitted Request MUST keep the same Identifier, and any new Request MUST change it. The peer MUST answer each Request, with a Response carrying the same Identifier, and never retransmits Responses on a timer. If a peer sees a duplicate Request it already answered, it MUST resend its Response; if it is still waiting for user input, it MUST silently discard the duplicate.

Because users may need to type, the RFC suggests a default retransmission timer of 6 seconds with a maximum of 10 retransmissions, possibly longer for token cards.

Success and Failure are not acknowledged and may be lost. A peer MUST allow for this: a Network Protocol packet can serve as an alternative sign of Success, and an LCP Terminate-Request can be taken as Failure. An authenticator may issue several Requests before a Failure, to allow for typing mistakes.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask a question and hear nothing, you ask again with the same question number. The answerer repeats a lost answer, but never nags you.

sections.title: The Initial Request and Response Types
sections.content:
Types 1 to 6 are defined here, and all implementations MUST support types 1 to 4. More types may come in follow-on documents.

  • Identity (1) asks who the peer is, usually as the first Request; an unknown identity is sent as zero bytes.
  • Notification (2) carries a displayable message such as a password about to expire, and is acknowledged with an empty Response.
  • Nak (3) is for Responses only. It says the requested authentication type is unacceptable and may name the one the peer wants.
  • MD5-Challenge (4) is analogous to CHAP with MD5; every implementation MUST support it.
  • One-Time Password (5) carries an OTP challenge and a response of 6 words from the OTP dictionary.
  • Generic Token Card (6) carries an ASCII text message and the token card data the user enters.

The RFC suggests retrying the Identity Request at least 3 times before sending a Failure.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP has a small set of question styles: who are you, a note for you, "I would rather do it another way", a secret-code challenge, and a button-code from a gadget.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security is the primary topic of the RFC, but it notes that how PPP authentication protocols interact is highly implementation dependent. Some implementations do not end the link on a failure and instead restrict traffic to a filtered subset.

There is no provision for retrying a failed authentication, though LCP can renegotiate the protocol at any time. Authentication need not be full duplex, and a different protocol may be used in each direction.

The RFC advises that a named user should have exactly one authentication method. Otherwise an attacker could push the negotiation to the weakest method, such as PAP rather than EAP. A user who needs several methods should use distinct identities, each tied to one method.
sections.plainLanguage: If a person can prove who they are in an easy way or a hard way, a thief will pick the easy way. So each person should have just one way to prove it.
